planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts in spring in lean, rocky, fast-draining soil in full sun after the last hard freeze.

directions: Blue sage is a rounded, silvery-leaved subshrub native to rocky slopes and pinyon-juniper woodlands of the Mojave Desert transition zone in Southern California, Nevada, and Arizona at elevations between roughly 4,000 and 8,000 feet, which gives it unusual cold hardiness for a desert sage. Its dense, felted foliage releases a strong, resinous fragrance when brushed, and from midsummer into fall it produces spikes of rose-purple bracts surrounding smaller violet-blue flowers that draw hummingbirds, bumblebees, and native carpenter bees. Because seed set is sparse and germination unreliable in cultivation, propagation is almost always by stem cuttings taken in late spring or fall. Give it gravelly, alkaline soil with sharp drainage and withhold summer water once established, as root rot in humid or heavy soils is its main limiting factor.

planting.note: Direct sow scarified seed into lean, well-drained soil in spring after danger of hard frost has passed.

directions: Narrowleaf globemallow is an upright, gray-green perennial of dry plains, roadsides, and open grassland from Texas and Oklahoma west through New Mexico and Arizona into the Chihuahuan and Sonoran Desert borderlands. Slender, willow-like leaves distinguish it from its broader-leaved globemallow relatives, and it carries loose spikes of cup-shaped flowers ranging from soft apricot-orange to lavender-pink over an unusually long season, from late spring through fall frost. It serves as a larval host for painted lady and other skipper butterflies and its pollen is a preferred forage of Sphaeralcea-specialist bees, in addition to general bumblebee and honeybee visitation. Once established in poor, rocky, or clay-loam soils it needs no supplemental water and tolerates hard pruning in late winter to keep growth compact.

planting.note: Scatter seed on bare, sandy soil in fall so it can germinate with cool-season rains and overwinter as a low rosette.

directions: Devil's lantern is a low, sprawling desert annual or short-lived biennial of sandy flats and dunes across the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts, forming a flat winter rosette that bolts into a many-branched plant studded with large, four-petaled white flowers that open at dusk and fade to pink by the following morning. The big, fragrant blooms are pollinated primarily by nocturnal hawkmoths, and the plant also attracts specialist Oenothera bees active at dawn before the flowers fully close. As the season ends the dried, papery stems curl inward around the seed capsules to form a distinctive rounded cage, which gives the plant both of its common names and makes attractive dried material for habitat displays. Sow directly into sandy, low-fertility soil with sharp drainage, since it will not tolerate transplanting or rich, moisture-retentive beds.

planting.note: Broadcast seed in fall directly among an established stand of native grasses or Artemisia, since seedlings must attach to a host plant's roots within their first year to survive.

directions: Wholeleaf Indian paintbrush is a clump-forming perennial of dry rocky slopes, piñon-juniper woodland, and short-grass prairie from the southern Rocky Mountains through Arizona and New Mexico, distinguished from other regional paintbrushes by its undivided, entire leaf margins and brilliant orange-red bracts that appear from spring into midsummer. Like all Castilleja, it is a hemiparasite that taps into the root systems of nearby grasses, sagebrush, or buckwheat for water and minerals, so seed is best broadcast into an already-planted native bed rather than grown alone in isolated pots. Established plants are a major early-season hummingbird and butterfly nectar source in high-desert gardens and are largely deer- and rabbit-resistant. Because of its parasitic root dependency, transplanting mature plants is rarely successful; direct seeding onto a compatible host planting gives the most reliable results.
sources: Native Plant Society of New Mexico

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants in fall so roots establish over the mild coastal winter ahead of the spring bloom flush.

directions: California bush sunflower is a fast-growing, soft-leaved subshrub of coastal sage scrub from Santa Barbara south into Baja California, producing a mounded flush of golden-yellow daisy flowers with dark centers from late winter through early summer, sometimes reblooming after rain. It is among the most reliable nectar and pollen sources for native bees and butterflies during California's late-winter bloom gap, when few other perennials are flowering, and it also provides cover and seed for birds. Plants are naturally short-lived, typically fading after five to eight years, but cutting stems back hard by half after the main bloom keeps growth dense and extends vigor, and it roots readily from cuttings if replacements are needed. It thrives in poor, rocky, or clay soils with excellent drainage and needs no irrigation once established, though a hard freeze below the mid-20s F will damage or kill top growth.

planting.note: Nick or soak scarified seed and direct sow in spring into rocky or caliche soil in full sun once the ground has warmed.

directions: Featherplume is a small, wiry-branched, nitrogen-fixing legume shrub of limestone hills, caliche flats, and rocky canyons across the Chihuahuan Desert from West Texas and southern New Mexico into northern Mexico. Its bicolor pea flowers, magenta fading to cream, open in flushes from spring through fall after rain and are followed by silky, feather-tipped seed plumes that catch the light and give the plant both its common name and extended ornamental interest into winter. It is a larval host for several native skipper butterflies and its flowers draw a steady stream of small native bees. Once rooted it is extremely drought- and heat-tolerant, needs no fertilizer thanks to its nitrogen-fixing nodules, and rarely requires pruning beyond an occasional shaping after the main spring bloom.
